source.title: Codebook Features: Sparse and Discrete Interpretability for Neural Networks
source.authors: Alex Tamkin; Mohammad Taufeeque; Noah D. Goodman

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neuron-level interpretability and compares neurons with learned code features, but does not test any listed version: it does not audit neuron-pole job shares, evaluate the specified neuron explanations, or build neuron attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: Figure 6 reports a comparison of code and neuron classifiers for regular-expression-defined features; these results are recorded under fits_no_version because they are not the pole-share audit or the explanation evaluations specified in V1–V7. Language-model performance, code-steering, and FSM state-intervention results do not measure the listed claim versions. Results from cited studies are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces codebook features, a vector-quantization bottleneck added by finetuning. Its only neuron results compare its own codes against neurons as classifiers of selected features. That comparison is not an audit of how many neuron poles have one job (V1, V2). It does not evaluate neuron explanations from activating examples or by simulation (V6, V7). It does not examine InceptionV1 (V3), architecture or tool effects on neuron interpretability (V4), or neuron attribution graphs (V5). The neuron precision numbers measure a related but different construct: the best single neuron's precision on code-defined features at matched recall.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is right. Codebook bottlenecks cost modest performance and give interpretable, steerable codes. In preliminary comparisons, codes beat the best neuron at classifying selected features. The authors also claim codes mitigate superposition in TokFSM.
record.recipe_differences: The study finetunes networks with sparse, discrete vector-quantization codebooks and compares code classifiers with neuron classifiers; it does not perform a neuron-pole audit or the explanation-testing methods described in the claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: In the 4-layer TokFSM model, state codes classify states with average precision 97.1%. The best neuron reaches 70.5% at matched recall.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a toy model with more features than neurons, single neurons are less precise detectors of known latent states than learned discrete codes.

fits_no_version.finding: For regex-defined features chosen from interpretable codes in a 410M WikiText-103 model, codes had over 30% higher average precision than the best neuron.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For simple textual features selected via codebook codes, the best single neuron is a less precise classifier than the code.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors note that top-activating tokens for TokFSM MLP neurons do not appear to follow any consistent pattern. This is anecdotal (Section 3.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons in a small superposition-forced toy transformer appear uninterpretable by top activations.

record.problems: The neuron-level interpretability comparison is preliminary. The authors note that regular expressions are imperfect proxies and that selecting codes for which they could form meaningful interpretations may bias the comparison in favor of codes.
record.rows_left_out: No other results are direct measurements of the listed versions. The paper's model-performance tables and code-steering and FSM-intervention results concern codebook models and are not neuron-pole audits or tests of the specified neuron explanations or attribution graphs.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job shares (~90% one job, ~7% two related jobs, 2–4% not understood).
Neuron-pole shares in other dense or mixture-of-experts models and across scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization.
Effect of architecture, regularization or tools on the share of interpretable neurons; the vision-model estimates.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
Whether explanations fit to activating examples predict where neurons fire.

record.verdict_notes: These are own-method-versus-neuron baselines in a codebook-finetuned model, not evaluations of neuron explanations. They should stay out of the version verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job shares and the stated one-job, two-job, and not-understood proportions.
Whether those neuron-pole shares generalize across models, architectures, or scales up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose, and recursive generalization.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain late-layer interpretability, including the stated InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples fail to predict neuron activations on other examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: k = 1 Attn+MLP codebook TokFSM model
rows.operation_detail: Compared code-classifier precision with the best neuron precision at matched recall for state features.

conditions.value: best neuron thresholded to match code recall

rows.baseline: Best-neuron precision at the code classifier's recall
rows.value: Codes: average precision 97.1%; average best-neuron precision 70.5%
rows.note: The authors report these as averages for the code-versus-neuron comparison; they do not report the share of neurons with a single interpretable job.
rows.check: This row compares the study's own method (codes) against neurons. It should not be a claim row. The subject is a 4-layer toy TokFSM model with 100 states and 1000 trigram features over 128 neurons, so superposition is forced by design. Best-neuron precision (70.5%) on code-matched features is not a neuron-job share.

rows.subject: 24-layer 410M parameter WikiText-103 model
rows.operation_detail: Compared code-classifier precision with the best neuron precision at matched recall for selected textual features.

conditions.value: best neuron thresholded to match code recall

rows.baseline: Best-neuron precision at the code classifier's recall
rows.value: Codes had over 30% higher average precision than neurons
rows.locator: Figure 6b; Section 4, Comparison to neuron-level interpretability
rows.note: The paper does not state the exact average precision values in the text. The experiment selected codes with apparently simple activation patterns and compared them against regular expressions.
rows.check: This row also compares the study's own method against neurons. Features were picked because codes looked interpretable, and regexes were built for them (authors note a possible bias, E.7). The subject is a codebook-finetuned Pythia-410M; it is unclear whether the neurons searched sit in that codebook model. Exact values are given only in Figure 6b.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
